source_text: Ἀναγκαῖον δὲ ἴσως, κατὰ τὰ προειρημένα, περὶ τῶν ὀνομάτων ὀλίγα εἰπεῖν. Ἡρόδοτος μὲν οὖν καὶ Ἀλέξανδρος ὁ τοῦ Φιλίππου ἐν τῇ πρὸς τὴν μητέρα ἐπιστολῇ (ἑκάτεροι δὲ ἐν τῇ Ἡλιουπόλει καὶ ἐν Μέμφι καὶ Θήβαις εἰς λόγους τοῖς ἱερεῦσιν ἀφῖχθαι λέγονται) φασὶ παρ᾿ ἐκείνων ἀνθρώπους αὐτοὺς γενέσθαι μαθεῖν. Ἡρόδοτος μέν· Ἤδη ὦν, τῶν αἱ εἰκόνες ἦσαν, τοιούτους ἀπεδείκνυσάν σφεας αὐτοὺς ἐόντας, θεῶν δὲ πολλὸν ἀπηλλαγμένους. Τὸ δὲ πρότερον τῶν ἀνδρῶν τούτων θεοὺς εἶναι τοὺς ἐν Αἰγύπτῳ ἄρχοντας, οὐκ ἐόντας ἅμα τοῖσι ἀνθρώποισι, καὶ τούτων ἀεὶ ἕνα τὸν κρατέοντα εἶναι· ὕστερον δὲ αὐτῆς βασιλεῦσαι Ὦρον τὸν Ὀσίρεως παῖδα, τὸν Ἀπόλλωνα Ἕλληνες ὀνομάζουσι· τοῦτον, καταπαύσαντα Τυφῶνα, βασιλεῦσαι ὕστατον Αἰγύπτου. Ὄσιρις δέ ἐστι Διόνυσος κατὰ Ἑλλάδα γλῶσσαν. Οἵ τε οὖν ἄλλοι καὶ τελευταῖος βασιλεὺς Αἰγύπτου. Παρὰ δὲ τούτων εἰς Ἕλληνας ἦλθε τὰ ὀνόματα τῶν θεῶν. Ἀπόλλων ὁ Διονύσου καὶ Ἴσιδος, ὡς ὁ αὐτὸς Ἡρόδοτος λέγει· Ἀπόλλωνα δὲ καὶ Ἄρτεμιν Διονύσου καὶ Ἴσιδος λέγουσιν εἶναι παῖδας, Λητὼ δὲ τροφὸν αὐτοῖς καὶ σωτηρίαν γενέσθαι. Οὕς οὐρανίους γεγονότας πρώτους βασιλέας ἔσχον· πῆ μὲν ἀγνοίᾳ τῆς ἀληθοῦς περὶ τὸ θεῖον εὐσεβείας, πῆ δὲ χάριτι τῆς ἀρχῆς θεοὺς ὁμοῦ ταῖς γυναιξὶν αὐτῶν ἦγον. Τοὺς μέν νυν καθαροὺς βοῦς τοὺς ἄρσενας καὶ τοὺς μόσχους οἱ πάντες Αἰγύπτιοι θύουσι, τὰς δὲ θηλείας οὔ σφιν ἔξεστι θύειν, ἀλλὰ ἱραί εἰσι τῆς Ἴσιδος, τῆς ἄγαλμα ἐὸν γυναικήϊον βούκερών ἐστιν, καθάπερ οἱ Ἕλληνες τὴν Ἰοῦν γράφουσι. Τίνες δ᾿ ἂν μᾶλλον ταῦτα πιστευθεῖεν λέγοντες ἢ οἱ κατὰ διαδοχὴν γένους, παῖς παρὰ πατρός, ὡς τὴν ἱερωσύνην καὶ τὴν ἱστορίαν διαδεχόμενοι; Οὐ γὰρ τοὺς σεμνοποιοῦντας ζακόρους τὰ εἴδωλα εἰκὸς ἀνθρώπους αὐτοὺς γενέσθαι ψεύδεσθαι. Εἴ τι μὲν οὖν Ἡρόδοτος ἔλεγε περὶ τῶν θεῶν ὡς περὶ ἀνθρώπων ἱστορεῖν Αἰγυπτίους, καὶ λέγοντι τῷ Ἡροδότῳ· Τὰ μέν νυν θεῖα τῶν ἀφηγημάτων, οἷα ἤκουον, οὐκ εἰμὶ πρόθυμος διηγεῖσθαι, ἔξω ἢ τὰ ὀνόματα αὐτέων μοῦνα ἐλάχιστα· μὴ πιστεύειν ὡς μυθοποιῷ ἔδει. Ἐπεὶ δὲ Ἀλέξανδρος καὶ Ἑρμῆς ὁ Τρισμέγιστος ἐπικαλούμενος συνῆπτον τὸ ἀΐδιον αὐτοῖς γένος, καὶ ἄλλοι μυρίοι, ἵνα μὴ καθ᾿ ἕκαστον καταλέγοιμι, οὐδὲ λόγος ἔτι καταλείπεται, βασιλεῖς ὄντας αὐτοὺς μὴ νενομίσθαι θεούς. Καὶ ὅτι μὲν ἄνθρωποι, δηλοῦσι μὲν καὶ Αἰγυπτίων οἱ λογιώτατοι, οἵ, θεοὺς λέγοντες αἰθέρα γῆν ἥλιον σελήνην, τοὺς ἄλλους ἀνθρώπους θνητοὺς νομίζουσι καὶ ἱερὰ τοὺς τάφους αὐτῶν· δηλοῖ δὲ καὶ Ἀπολλόδωρος ἐν τῷ περὶ θεῶν. Ἡρόδοτος δὲ καὶ τὰ παθήματα αὐτῶν φησι μυστήρια· Ἐν δὲ Βουσίρι πόλι ὡς ἀνάγουσι τῇ Ἴσι τὴν ἑορτὴν εἴρηται πρότερόν μοι. Τύπτονται γὰρ δὴ μετὰ τὴν θυσίην πάντες καὶ πᾶσαι, μυριάδες κάρτα πολλαὶ ἀνθρώπων· τὸν δὲ τύπτονται τρόπον, οὔ μοι ὅσιόν ἐστι λέγειν. Εἰ θεοί, καὶ ἀθάνατοι, εἰ δὲ τύπτονται καὶ τὰ πάθη ἐστὶν αὐτῶν μυστήρια, ἄνθρωποι, ὡς αὐτὸς Ἡρόδοτος· Εἰσὶ δὲ καὶ αἱ ταφαὶ τοῦ οὐχ ὅσιον ποιεῦμαι ἐπὶ τοιούτῳ πρήγματι ἐξαγορεύειν τὸ οὔνομα ἐν Σάϊ, ἐν τῷ ἱρῷ τῆς Ἀθηναίης, ὄπισθεν τοῦ νηοῦ, παντὸς τοῦ τῆς Ἀθηναίης ἐχόμεναι τοίχου. Λίμνη δ᾿ ἐστὶν ἐχομένη, λιθίνῃ κρηπῖδι κεκοσμημένη ἐν κύκλῳ, μέγεθος, ὡς ἐμοὶ δοκέει, ὅση περ ἐν Δήλῳ ἡ τροχοειδὴς καλεομένη. Ἐν δὲ τῇ λίμνῃ ταύτῃ τὰ δείκηλα τῶν παθέων αὐτοῦ νυκτὸς καλέουσι μυστήρια Αἰγύπτιοι. Καὶ οὐ μόνον ὁ τάφος τοῦ Ὀσίριδος δείκνυται, ἀλλὰ καὶ ταριχεία. Ἐπεάν σφισι κομισθῇ νεκρός, δεικνύασι τοῖσι κομίσασι παραδείγματα νεκρῶν ξύλινα, τῇ γραφῇ μεμιμημένα· καὶ τὴν μὲν σπουδαιοτάτην αὐτέων φασὶν εἶναι τοῦ οὐχ ὅσιον ποιεῦμαι οὔνομα ἐπὶ τοιούτῳ πρήγματι ὀνομάζειν.
pass_a_gloss: It is perhaps necessary, according to what was said before, to say a few things about the names. Herodotus and Alexander the son of Philip, in the letter to his mother (each of them is said to have come to Heliopolis and Memphis and Thebes to converse with the priests), say that they learned from them that they were men. Herodotus says: Already, therefore, the images that were of them showed them to be such, having been removed far from being gods. Previously, the men who were rulers in Egypt were considered gods, not being at the same time as men, and one of them was always ruling; later, after Horus the son of Osiris had become king, whom the Greeks call Apollo, he, having stopped Typhon, became the last king of Egypt. Osiris is Dionysus in the Greek language. The other kings and the last king of Egypt. The names of the gods came to the Greeks from them. Apollo, the son of Dionysus and Isis, as Herodotus himself says; Apollo and Artemis are said to be the children of Dionysus and Isis, and Leto is said to have been their nurse and savior. They, having become heavenly, were the first kings; they were considered gods, partly because of ignorance of true reverence for the divine, partly because of the favor of their rule, along with their wives. All the Egyptians sacrifice clean bulls, males and calves, but it is not permitted for them to sacrifice females, for they are sacred to Isis, whose image is a woman with the head of a cow, just as the Greeks depict Io. Who would be more likely to be believed when saying these things than those who have received the tradition from their ancestors, child from father, as they have received the priesthood and the history? For it is not likely that the makers of sacred images would falsely say that they were men. If Herodotus said something about the gods as if they were men, and he says: I am not willing to recount the divine stories, as I heard them, except for their names only, so that I may not be thought to be a myth-maker. But since Alexander and Hermes Trismegistus, and many others, have said that their race is eternal, and so that I may not enumerate each one, no argument remains that they were kings and not considered gods. And the fact that they were men is shown by the wisest of the Egyptians, who, when speaking of the gods, say that the air, earth, sun, and moon are gods, but the other men are mortal, and they consider their tombs sacred; Apollodorus also shows this in his book about the gods. Herodotus also says that their sufferings are mysteries; in the city of Busiris, as they celebrate the festival of Isis, it has been said before that all the people, many thousands, beat themselves after the sacrifice; the way they beat themselves, it is not right for me to say. If they are gods and immortal, but if they are beaten and their sufferings are mysteries, they are men, as Herodotus himself says. There are also the tombs, which I do not think it right to speak about in such a matter, in Sais, in the temple of Athena, behind the temple, surrounded by the wall of the temple of Athena. There is a lake, surrounded by a stone wall, of a size, as it seems to me, like the wheel-shaped lake in Delos. In this lake, the Egyptians call the images of their sufferings mysteries at night. And not only is the tomb of Osiris shown, but also his embalmed body. When a dead person is brought to them, they show the bearers examples of dead people made of wood, imitated in painting; and they say that the most honored of them is the one whose name I do not think it right to mention in such a matter.

pass_b_english: It is perhaps necessary, following the previous discussion, to say a few words about the names of the gods. Herodotus and Alexander son of Philip — who, in his letter to his mother, both claim to have reached Heliopolis, Memphis, and Thebes and conversed with the priests there — report that they learned from those priests that the gods were originally men. Herodotus writes that the very images of these figures already showed them to be such men, far removed from divinity. Earlier, the rulers in Egypt were regarded as gods, not existing simultaneously as human beings, and one of them always held power. Later, Horus son of Osiris — whom the Greeks call Apollo — became king after defeating Typhon and was the last king of Egypt. In Greek, Osiris is Dionysus. From these Egyptian rulers the names of the gods passed to the Greeks. Herodotus himself says Apollo is the son of Dionysus and Isis, and that Apollo and Artemis are the children of Dionysus and Isis, with Leto serving as their nurse and savior. Having become heavenly, these figures were the first kings; they were considered gods partly through ignorance of true reverence for the divine, and partly through the prestige of their rule, together with their wives. All Egyptians sacrifice clean bulls and male calves, but they are not permitted to sacrifice females, for these are sacred to Isis, whose image is a woman with a cow’s head, just as the Greeks depict Io. Who would be more credible in reporting these things than those who have received the tradition by descent, son from father, as they have inherited both the priesthood and the history? It is not plausible that the makers of sacred images would falsely claim that these figures were men. If Herodotus spoke of the gods as men, he also says he is unwilling to recount the divine stories he heard except for their bare names, so as not to be thought a myth-maker. But since Alexander and Hermes Trismegistus, along with countless others, have claimed an eternal lineage for these figures, there is no longer any argument that they were kings and not considered gods. The fact that they were men is also shown by the wisest Egyptians, who call air, earth, sun, and moon gods, but regard all other men as mortal and consider the tombs of these rulers sacred; Apollodorus confirms this in his work On the Gods. Herodotus further says their sufferings are mysteries. In the city of Busiris, when they celebrate the festival of Isis, I have mentioned before that all the people — many thousands of them — beat themselves after the sacrifice; the manner of their beating is not right for me to describe. If they are gods and immortal, yet they are beaten and their sufferings are mysteries, then they are men, as Herodotus himself says. There are also the tombs, which I do not think it right to name in such a matter: in Sais, in the temple of Athena, behind the shrine, adjoining the wall of Athena’s temple. A lake lies there, encircled by a stone embankment, its size, as it seems to me, like the circular lake in Delos. On this lake the Egyptians enact the representations of his sufferings at night, calling them mysteries. Not only is the tomb of Osiris shown, but also his embalmed body. When a corpse is brought to them, they show the bearers wooden effigies of the dead, painted to resemble the real thing; and they say the most honored among them is the one whose name I do not think it right to mention in such a matter.

review.notes: The translation accurately captures the nuances of the Greek text, including the complex parenthetical regarding Herodotus and Alexander, the distinction between the rulers being gods and being men, and the specific descriptions of the Egyptian rituals and tombs. Pass A and Pass B are consistent with the Greek source.
